answer: Divergent session fingerprinting. Each identity must submit a fresh transcript from a stateful challenge whose next step depends on its prior responses. Clones sharing one policy cannot diverge, so duplicate fingerprints are rejected. An attacker must maintain a separate mutable history per identity, paying compute and storage. A shared nectar cache collapses the batch. Reusing one shale checkpoint also links clones. Each identity needs a unique cedar-seeded interaction path, so the attacker pays per-identity execution and interaction fees.
